Date and time (UTC): First launch of NASA and NOAA joint science mission under the NLS II launch contract (not related to NASA CRS or USAF OSP3 contracts) and last launch of the Falcon 9 v1.1 launch vehicle. The Jason-3 satellite was successfully deployed to target orbit.[101] SpaceX attempted for the first time to recover the first-stage booster on its new Pacific autonomous drone ship, but after a soft landing on the ship, the lockout on one of the landing legs failed to latch and the booster fell over and exploded.[102][103]

Date and time (UTC): Second launch of the enhanced Falcon 9 Full Thrust launch vehicle.[94] SpaceX attempted for the first time to recover a booster from a GTO launch to a drone ship.[107] Successful landing was not expected due to low fuel reserves[108] and the booster "landed hard".[109] But the controlled-descent, atmospheric re-entry and navigation to the drone ship were successful and returned significant test data on bringing back high-energy Falcon 9 boosters.[110]

Date and time (UTC): Dragon carried over 1,500 kg (3,300 lb) of supplies and delivered the inflatable Bigelow Expandable Activity Module (BEAM) to the ISS for two years of in-orbit tests.[113] The rocket's first stage landed smoothly on SpaceX's autonomous spaceport drone ship at 9 minutes after liftoff, making this the first successful landing of a rocket booster on a ship at sea from an orbital launch.[114] The first stage B1021 later became the first orbital booster to be reused when it launched SES-10 on 30 March 2017.[5] A month later, the Dragon spacecraft returned a downmass containing astronaut's Scott Kelly biological samples from his year-long mission on ISS.[115](more details)

Date and time (UTC): One year after pioneering this technique on Flight 16, Falcon again launched two Boeing 702SP gridded ion thruster satellites at 1,800 kg (4,000 lb) each,[129][130] in a dual-stack configuration, with the two customers sharing the rocket and mission costs.[78] First-stage landing attempt on drone ship failed due to low thrust on one of the three landing engines;[131] a sub-optimal path led to the stage running out of propellant just above the deck of the landing ship,[132] slamming to the drone ship, breaking a leg, and falling over.

Date and time (UTC): The rocket and the AMOS-6 payload were lost in a launch pad explosion on 1 September 2016, during propellant filling procedures before a static fire test.[138][139] The pad was clear of personnel, and there were no injuries.[140] SpaceX released an official statement in January 2017, indicating that the cause of the failure was a buckled liner in several of the composite overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) (used to store helium which pressurizes the stage's propellant tanks), causing perforations that allowed liquid and/or solid oxygen to accumulate underneath the lining, which was ignited by friction.[141] Following the explosion, SpaceX has switched to performing static fire tests only without attached payloads.(more details)
